questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Jacobian Determinant of a Transformation
questions.problem:
Find the Jacobian determinant of the transformation $T,$ defined as

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}3u+2v \\ u+3v\end{aligned}].
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Given a transformation 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}],
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have $x(u,v)=3u+2v$ and $y(u,v)=u+3v.$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =3 & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =2 \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =1 & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}3 & 2 \\ 1 & 3\end{aligned}| \\  & =3\cdot 3-1\cdot 2 \\  & =9-2 \\  & =7.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Find the Jacobian determinant of the transformation $T([\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}])=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(u+v) \\ 4u+6v\end{aligned}].$
questions.worked_solution:
Given a transformation 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}],
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have $x=\operatorname{cos}⁡(u+v)$ and $y=4u+6v.$ 

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡(u+v) & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡(u+v) \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =4 & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =6\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{sin}⁡(u+v) & -\operatorname{sin}⁡(u+v) \\ \,\text{ }4\, & \,\text{ }6\end{aligned}| \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡(u+v)\cdot 6-(-\operatorname{sin}⁡(u+v))\cdot 4 \\  & =-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(u+v).\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Jacobian Determinant of a Transformation
questions.problem:
Find the Jacobian determinant of the transformation $T,$ defined as

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}2u\operatorname{cos}⁡v \\ 3u\operatorname{sin}⁡v\end{aligned}].
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Given a transformation 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}],
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have $x(u,v)=2u\operatorname{cos}⁡v$ and $y(u,v)=3u\operatorname{sin}⁡v.$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡v & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =-2u\operatorname{sin}⁡v \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =3\operatorname{sin}⁡v & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =3u\operatorname{cos}⁡v\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{cos}⁡v & -2u\operatorname{sin}⁡v \\ 3\operatorname{sin}⁡v & 3u\operatorname{cos}⁡v\end{aligned}| \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡v\cdot 3u\operatorname{cos}⁡v-(-2u\operatorname{sin}⁡v)\cdot 3\operatorname{sin}⁡v \\  & =6u({cos}^{2}⁡v+{cos}^{2}⁡v) \\  & =6u.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Find the Jacobian determinant of the transformation $T([\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}])=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(u+v) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(u-v)\end{aligned}].$
questions.worked_solution:
Given a transformation 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}],
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Here, we have $x=\operatorname{sin}⁡(u+v)$ and $y=\operatorname{cos}⁡(u-v).$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(u+v) & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(u+v) \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡(u-v) & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(u-v)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(u+v) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(u+v) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(u-v)\, & \operatorname{sin}⁡(u-v)\end{aligned}| \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(u+v)\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(u-v)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(u+v)\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡(u-v)) \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡(u+v)\operatorname{sin}⁡(u-v).\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Find the Jacobian determinant of the transformation $T([\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}])=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{u+v} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(uv)\end{aligned}].$
questions.worked_solution:
Given a transformation 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}],
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have $x(u,v)={e}^{u+v}$ and $y(u,v)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(uv).$  

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & ={e}^{u+v} & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & ={e}^{u+v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =\frac{1}{u} & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =\frac{1}{v}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}{e}^{u+v} & {e}^{u+v} \\ \frac{1}{u} & \frac{1}{v}\end{aligned}| \\  & ={e}^{u+v}\cdot (\frac{1}{v})-{e}^{u+v}\cdot (\frac{1}{u}) \\  & =\frac{{e}^{u+v}}{v}-\frac{{e}^{u+v}}{u} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{u+v}(u-v)}{vu}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
For the transformation $T,$ defined as

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}{e}^{u+v} \\ {e}^{u-v}\end{aligned}].
$$

compute the value of the Jacobian determinant at the point where $[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -5\end{aligned}].$
questions.worked_solution:
Given a transformation 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}],
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have $x(u,v)={e}^{u+v}$ and $y(u,v)={e}^{u-v}.$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & ={e}^{u+v} & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & ={e}^{u+v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & ={e}^{u-v} & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =-{e}^{u-v}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}{e}^{u+v} & {e}^{u+v} \\ {e}^{u-v} & -{e}^{u-v}\end{aligned}| \\  & ={e}^{u+v}\cdot (-{e}^{u-v})-{e}^{u+v}\cdot {e}^{u-v} \\  & =-{e}^{2u}-{e}^{2u} \\  & =-2{e}^{2u}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, when $[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -5\end{aligned}],$ the value of our Jacobian determinant is

$$
{\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|}_{(0,-5)}=-2{e}^{2(0)}=-2.
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Evaluating a Jacobian Determinant
questions.problem:
For the transformation $T,$ defined as 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}uv \\ \frac{v}{u}\end{aligned}]
$$

 

compute the value of the Jacobian determinant at the point where $[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 3\end{aligned}].$
questions.worked_solution:
Given a transformation 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}],
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have $x=uv$ and $y=\frac{v}{u}.$ 

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =v & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =u \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =-\frac{v}{{u}^{2}} & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =\frac{1}{u}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}v & u \\ -\frac{v}{{u}^{2}}\, & \frac{1}{u}\end{aligned}| \\  & =v\cdot \frac{1}{u}\text{ }-u\cdot (-\frac{v}{{u}^{2}}) \\  & =\frac{2v}{u}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, when $[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 3\end{aligned}],$ the value of our Jacobian determinant is

$$
{\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|}_{(-2,3)}=\frac{2(3)}{-2}=-3.
$$

questions.problem:
For the transformation $T,$ defined as

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡u \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡v\end{aligned}]
$$

compute the value of the Jacobian determinant at the point where $[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\pi /6 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$
questions.worked_solution:
Given a transformation 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}],
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have $x(u,v)=\operatorname{cos}⁡u$ and $y(u,v)=\operatorname{sin}⁡v.$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡u & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =0 \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =0 & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡v\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{sin}⁡u & 0 \\ 0 & \operatorname{cos}⁡v\end{aligned}| \\  & =(-\operatorname{sin}⁡u)\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡v-0\cdot 0 \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡u\operatorname{cos}⁡v.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, when $[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\pi /6 \\ 0\end{aligned}],$ the value of our Jacobian determinant is

$$
{\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|}_{(\frac{\pi }{6},0)}=-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6})\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)=-\frac{1}{2}.
$$

questions.problem:
For the transformation $T,$ defined as

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}\frac{{u}^{2}-{v}^{2}}{2} \\ uv\end{aligned}]
$$

compute the value of the Jacobian determinant at the point where $[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -2\end{aligned}].$
questions.worked_solution:
Given a transformation 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}],
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have $x(u,v)=\frac{{u}^{2}-{v}^{2}}{2}$ and $y(u,v)=uv.$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =u & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =-v \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =v & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =u\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}u & -v \\ v & u\end{aligned}| \\  & =u\cdot u-(-v)\cdot v \\  & ={u}^{2}+{v}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, when $[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -2\end{aligned}],$ the value of our Jacobian determinant is

$$
{\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|}_{(-1,-2)}=(-1)^{2}+(-2)^{2}=5.
$$

questions.problem:
For the transformation $T,$ defined as

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}{e}^{u-v} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(uv)\end{aligned}].
$$

compute the value of the Jacobian determinant at the point where $[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$
questions.worked_solution:
Given a transformation 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}],
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have $x(u,v)={e}^{u-v}$ and $y(u,v)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(uv).$  

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & ={e}^{u-v} & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =-{e}^{u-v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =\frac{1}{u} & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =\frac{1}{v}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}{e}^{u-v} & -{e}^{u-v} \\ \frac{1}{u} & \frac{1}{v}\end{aligned}| \\  & ={e}^{u-v}\cdot (\frac{1}{v})-(-{e}^{u-v})\cdot \frac{1}{u} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{u-v}}{v}+\frac{{e}^{u-v}}{u}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, when $[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],$ the value of our Jacobian determinant is

$$
{\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|}_{(1,1)}=\frac{{e}^{(1)-(1)}}{(1)}+\frac{{e}^{(1)-(1)}}{(1)}=2.
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Identifying the Local Area Scale Factor of a Transformation
questions.problem:
Consider a small rectangle $Δ$ whose bottom-left corner is located at the point $(-2,2)$ with sides parallel to the coordinate axes in the $uv$-plane and whose area is $\delta A.$ Which of the following gives the best approximation for the area of the image of this rectangle under the action of the transformation $T,$ given by

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}{e}^{u+v} \\ {u}^{3}+v\end{aligned}]?
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that the absolute value of the Jacobian determinant gives the local area scale factor of the transformation at that point:

$$
\text{Area}(T(Δ))≈|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\cdot {{\text{Area}(Δ)}_{⏟}}_{\delta A}
$$

 

Computing the corresponding Jacobian determinant, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}{e}^{u+v} & {e}^{u+v} \\ 3{u}^{2} & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & ={e}^{u+v}\cdot 1-3{u}^{2}\cdot {e}^{u+v} \\  & ={e}^{u+v}(1-3{u}^{2}) \\ {\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|}_{(-2,2)} & ={e}^{u+v}(1-3{u}^{2})\,{|}_{u=-2\,v=2} \\  & ={e}^{-2+2}(1-3(-2)^{2}) \\  & =-11\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(T(Δ)) & ≈|-11|\cdot \delta A \\  & =11\,\delta A.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Consider a small rectangle $Δ$ whose bottom-left corner is located at the point $(4,2)$ with sides parallel to the coordinate axes in the $uv$-plane and whose area is $\delta A.$ Which of the following gives the best approximation for the area of the image of this rectangle under the action of the transformation $T,$ given by

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}\sqrt{u}+{v}^{2} \\ uv\end{aligned}]?
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that the absolute value of the Jacobian determinant gives the local area scale factor of the transformation at that point:

$$
\text{Area}(T(Δ))≈|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\cdot {{\text{Area}(Δ)}_{⏟}}_{\delta A}
$$

 

Computing the corresponding Jacobian determinant, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2\sqrt{u}} & 2v \\ v & u\end{aligned}| \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{u}}\cdot u-v\cdot 2v \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{u}-2{v}^{2} \\ {\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|}_{(4,2)} & ={\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{u}-2{v}^{2}\,|}_{u=4\,v=2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{4}-2(2)^{2} \\  & =-7\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(T(Δ)) & ≈|-7|\cdot \delta A \\  & =7\,\delta A.\end{aligned}
$$

Consider a small rectangle $Δ$ whose bottom-left corner is located at the point $(-1,1)$ with sides parallel to the coordinate axes in the $uv$-plane and whose area is $\delta A.$ Which of the following gives the best approximation for the area of the image of this rectangle under the action of the transformation $T,$ given by

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}v{e}^{u} \\ u{e}^{v}\end{aligned}]?
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that the absolute value of the Jacobian determinant gives the local area scale factor of the transformation at that point:

$$
\text{Area}(T(Δ))≈|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\cdot {{\text{Area}(Δ)}_{⏟}}_{\delta A}
$$

 

Computing the corresponding Jacobian determinant, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}v{e}^{u} & {e}^{u} \\ {e}^{v} & u{e}^{v}\end{aligned}| \\  & =v{e}^{u}\cdot u{e}^{v}-{e}^{v}\cdot {e}^{u} \\  & =uv{e}^{u+v}-{e}^{u+v} \\  & =(uv-1){e}^{u+v} \\ {\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|}_{(-1,1)} & =(uv-1){e}^{u+v}\,{|}_{u=-1\,v=1} \\  & =(-1\cdot 1-1){e}^{-1+1} \\  & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(T(Δ)) & ≈|-2|\cdot \delta A \\  & =2\,\delta A.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Which of the following shows the region in the $uv$-plane where the transformation $T,$ given by 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}{u}^{2}-2{v}^{2} \\ u-v\end{aligned}],
$$

is (locally) orientation-reversing?
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that a transformation is (locally) orientation-reversing at the points where the Jacobian determinant is negative:

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}<0
$$

We have

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}{u}^{2}-2{v}^{2} \\ u-v\end{aligned}].
$$

Computing the corresponding Jacobian determinant, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}2u & -4v \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}| \\  & =2u\cdot (-1)-(-4v)\cdot 1 \\  & =-2u+4v.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the required regions, we solve the following inequality:

$$
\begin{aligned}-2u+4v & <0 \\ 4v & <2u \\ v & <\frac{1}{2}u\end{aligned}
$$

 

Notice that the equation 

$$
v=\frac{1}{2}u
$$

defines a straight line, and the coordinates of, say, $(1,-1)$ satisfy the inequality. 

Therefore, the region where the transformation is (locally) orientation-reversing must be the following:

canonical_examples.problem:
Find the Jacobian determinant of the transformation $\mathbf{T},$ defined as

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14043620/assets/ce4692599c5c9fe69ed9247d65dee5d982e1b7a2cf33b9070b799c94c321bad4.png)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Given a transformation 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14043620/assets/59265be9c026880542032006b0c4aec9f1c8eeb2cd448423d38c17f75e1393cd.png)

the Jacobian determinant of $\mathbf T,$ denoted $\dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} ,$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have $x=(u+v)^3$ and $y=(u-v)^2.$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =3(u+v)^{2} & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =3(u+v)^{2} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =2(u-v) & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =-2(u-v)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}3(u+v)^{2} & 3(u+v)^{2} \\ 2(u-v) & -2(u-v)\end{aligned}| \\  & =3(u+v)^{2}\cdot (-2(u-v))-3(u+v)^{2}\cdot 2(u-v) \\  & =-12(u+v)^{2}(u-v).\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
Consider a small rectangle $\Delta$ whose bottom-left corner is located at the point $(-1,2)$ with sides parallel to the coordinate axes in the $uv$-plane and whose area is $\delta{A}.$ Find an approximation for the area of the image of this rectangle under the action of the transformation $\mathbf T,$ given by
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14043620/assets/4c41597b6c647ba16bff7b6675d1bbe9d3c66b8cbb8e9a13bbb6651da6cd284e.png)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Recall that the absolute value of the Jacobian determinant gives the local area scale factor of the transformation at that point:

$$
\textrm{Area}\big(\mathbf{T}(\Delta)\big) \approx \left| \dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} \right| \cdot \underbrace{\textrm{Area}(\Delta)}_{\large \delta{A}}
$$

 

Computing the corresponding Jacobian determinant, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}{v}^{3} & 3u{v}^{2} \\ 2u & 2v\end{aligned}| \\  & ={v}^{3}\cdot 2v-3u{v}^{2}\cdot 2u \\  & =2{v}^{4}-6{u}^{2}{v}^{2} \\ {\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|}_{(-1,2)} & =(2{v}^{4}-6{u}^{2}{v}^{2})\,{|}_{u=-1\,v=2} \\  & =2(2)^{4}-6(-1)^{2}(2)^{2} \\  & =32-24 \\  & =8\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(T(Δ)) & ≈|8|\cdot \delta A \\  & =8\,\delta A.\end{aligned}
$$
